issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'full sensory reliving' suggests highly vivid, poorly contextualized trauma memory, which sits in marked tension with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' Those two can sometimes coexist, but as a three-item profile with shame on recall they pull in opposing directions and are clinically questionable together.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: 'Avoid enclosed spaces' is not clearly coherent with the rest of the profile for sexual assault as described here. The threat and memory items center on being followed, danger in unfamiliar places, delays, shame, and vivid reliving; enclosed spaces introduces a more specific situational avoidance that is not supported by the memory/threat content and looks disconnected from the formulation, especially since Triggers is not active in this case.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits in tension with 'When I remember the event I feel intense shame' and 'Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time.' Severe shame and terror on recall usually make disclosure difficult rather than easy, so this combination is clinically questionable within the same node.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: 'Ruminate about how to get even with assailant' is a poor fit with the rest of the profile for this trauma type and patient presentation. The Memory and Threat items emphasize shame, terror, hypervigilance, and avoidance, which is more consistent with fear-based post-assault PTSD; revenge-focused rumination pulls toward a different emotional/cognitive stance and lacks support elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: 'Gambling' is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly anchored to the rest of the presentation. The dominant active formulation is Memory↔Threat↔Maladaptive Strategies around trauma recollection and danger monitoring after sexual assault; gambling for excitement/distracting oneself is too nonspecific and does not connect clearly to the patient's other selected threat and memory items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Enclosed Spaces' appears to be a trigger/avoidance cue rather than a maladaptive strategy, and it is poorly matched to the rest of the profile. The threat and memory items center on being followed, danger in unfamiliar places, shame, terror, and speechless recall; avoidance of enclosed spaces is a different contextual pattern that is not otherwise supported here.

vignette: Reginald, a 53-year-old social worker, sat in his office, fidgeting with papers on his desk. His mind kept drifting back to that night five years ago when he was sexually assaulted by a stranger in a parking garage. The memory still felt like an open wound, and whenever it surfaced, Reginald was hit with intense shame and terror. He couldn't shake the feeling of vulnerability that lingered long after the assault. Reginald's wife had been worried about him for months, noticing how he would become withdrawn and irritable at random moments. What she didn't know was that Reginald had started to ruminate on ways to get even with his assailant. He would spend hours replaying the event in his head, thinking of all the things he could have done differently. The fantasies of revenge gave him a temporary sense of control, but ultimately left him feeling empty and consumed by anger. To cope with the anxiety that gripped him, Reginald started to avoid enclosed or confined spaces. He would take the stairs instead of the elevator, even if it meant climbing 20 floors. His colleagues noticed the change, but Reginald brushed it off as a desire for exercise. The truth was, he couldn't bear the feeling of being trapped. Reginald's work began to suffer as well. As a social worker, he often had to visit clients in unfamiliar neighborhoods. But since the assault, he found himself avoiding these visits or making excuses to stay in the office. His fear of not being able to assess potential dangers in new places had become overwhelming. Even simple tasks like grocery shopping became daunting challenges. Reginald's hypervigilance also started to affect his daily routine. He would frequently check behind him, expecting to see someone lurking in the shadows. When he was running late for a meeting or an appointment took longer than expected, Reginald's mind would start racing with worst-case scenarios. His brain had become wired to assume that delays were a sign of something bad happening. When memories of the assault surfaced, Reginald tried to push them out of his mind. He didn't want to relive the terror and shame, but it was hard to shake off. There were moments when he felt like he couldn't find words to describe what had happened. It was as if his brain had become stuck on that night, unable to process the trauma. Reginald's wife finally convinced him to seek help after she found him breaking down in tears one evening. He realized that he needed support to work through his emotions and develop healthier coping mechanisms. As Reginald sat in his therapist's office for the first time, he felt a glimmer of hope that he might be able to break free from the shackles of his trauma. What brought him to this point was the realization that his symptoms were affecting not just his personal life but also his work as a social worker. He couldn't bear the thought of continuing to live in fear, constantly looking over his shoulder or avoiding places and people. Reginald was scared of confronting the memories he had been trying to suppress for so long, but he knew it was necessary if he wanted to heal.
